strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: injecting 3D latent 'mentaling' tokens into VLM reasoning trajectories, trained without dense 3D annotations or external priors at inference, is a meaningful departure from pure-text/2D-cue reasoning and from tool-augmented approaches (e.g., Ego3D-VLM, MindCube).

Comprehensive empirical validation: the method is applied to three VLM families (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, LLaVA-OneVision-1.5) at many scales, evaluated on eight benchmarks (MindCube-Tiny, Ego3D-Bench, VSI-Bench, SPBench, CV-Bench, SPAR-Bench, ViewSpatial-Bench, MMSI-Bench), and consistently improves over both base VLMs and specialized spatial-reasoning baselines (Tables 1-3).
Useful ablations: latent size (Tab. 5), token placement (Tab. 6 shows a large 75.2 vs. 42.0 effect), projector direction, and each of the three RL rewards, giving insight into design choices.
The projector back to VGGT feature space and DPT-based point cloud visualization (Fig. 4) provides a concrete interpretability pathway, distinguishing the work from opaque latent-reasoning methods.

Cross-dataset generalization is demonstrated: training only on MindCube-derived data still improves Ego3D-Bench, and the model beats Ego3D-VLM without GroundingDINO/DepthAnything modules (Tab. 3), supporting the 'no external prior' claim.
weaknesses: Unclear whether the 3D latents function as a genuine reasoning medium. The latents are not autoregressively fed back into the model (admitted in Limitations), and the ablation shows placing them inside <think> collapses performance, suggesting the tokens act largely as a regularized side-channel rather than information the model actually conditions on for the answer. The paper does not include an experiment that isolates the causal contribution of the latent content (e.g., shuffling/corrupting latents at test time or training without alignment loss in S1).

Tension in the claims: the paper repeatedly states trajectory optimization uses 'solely outcome signals,' yet the RL reward includes r3D, a dense process reward computed against VGGT features (Eq. 12). This weakens the 'annotation-free/outcome-only' framing and should be stated more precisely.

Potential train-test proximity on the headline benchmark: CoT data is synthesized from the 10K MindCube training split and evaluated on MindCube-Tiny; while Ego3D results support generalization, the very large MindCube gains (up to 108.8%) are not analyzed for leakage or for sensitivity to GPT-4o-generated reasoning style.

Brittleness: performance collapses for latent sizes 32/64 (25.1/15.5) and for mid-trajectory token placement, indicating the framework is fragile to hyper-parameter choices; no variance/significance reporting across runs is given for RL results, which can be unstable.

Interpretability evidence is qualitative and thin: Fig. 4 point clouds are described as only 'roughly' depicting the scene, with no quantitative metric of reconstruction fidelity or prompt-relevance, so the claim that latents encode prompt-guided 3D scenes is under-supported.

Presentation issues: duplicate/incorrect baseline descriptions in Sec. 4.3 (both variants described as 'Aug-CGMap-FFR-Out'), a missing parenthesis in Eq. 7, ambiguous description of token placement relative to the Fig. 2 example (text says tokens go before <think>, but the figure shows them mid-reasoning), and the abstract's 'consistently outperforms strong baselines' overstates weaker sub-tasks (e.g., Travel Time, Obj. Rel. gains are small or flat).

Novelty positioning could be sharper: relative to Mirage [79] and LVR [31], the contribution is essentially moving latent supervision from 2D image embeddings to 3D foundation features; the paper should more carefully delineate what is new beyond the feature source.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and reasonably novel: inserting 3D 'mentaling' tokens into a VLM's reasoning trajectory and aligning their hidden states with a 3D foundation model (VGGT) via distillation, avoiding external depth/point-cloud priors at inference time. This differs from prior latent-reasoning work (Mirage, LVR) which targets 2D visual latents.

The two-stage training recipe (feature alignment SFT followed by outcome-based GRPO with a 3D-alignment reward) is clearly specified, including losses (Eqs. 5-9), rewards, and hyperparameters, which supports reproducibility.

The evaluation is broad: three VLM families (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, LLaVA-OneVision) at multiple scales, two spatial benchmarks plus six additional ones (VSI, SPBench, CV, SPAR, ViewSpatial, MMSI), and comparisons against multiple spatial-specialized baselines (Table 2) and Ego3D-VLM (Table 3).

Useful ablations are provided: latent size (Table 5), token placement, projector direction, and each RL reward component (Table 6), as well as training-strategy comparisons against cognitive-map SFT and SFT+RL baselines (Table 4).
The interpretability claim is partially supported: projected latents decoded through VGGT's DPT produce point clouds (Fig. 4) that roughly reflect the scene, which is a nice qualitative check.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim is under-supported. The 3D latents are not fed back into the model autoregressively (admitted in Limitations), so the causal role of the '3D mentaling' in producing correct answers is unclear—the special tokens may largely act as pause/compute tokens. There is no ablation removing or randomizing the 3D tokens at inference, or replacing the VGGT distillation target with a generic regularizer, which would be the decisive experiment.

Novelty claims are overstated. 'First to enable 3D mentaling ... without any 3D prior input' is misleading: the method depends heavily on VGGT (a 3D foundation model) during both training stages, including a 3D-feature reward in RL. The framework is best described as an incremental extension of Mirage's latent-token recipe from 2D to 3D-aligned latents; a direct head-to-head comparison with Mirage or LVR on these benchmarks is missing.

Potential confound in the headline results: training data is generated by GPT-4o distillation on the MindCube training split, and the largest gains are reported on MindCube-Tiny (75.2 vs. 33.2 for Qwen2.5-VL-3B). The paper does not fully disentangle how much of the gain comes from strong GPT-4o CoT distillation versus the 3D latent mechanism; a CoT-SFT+GRPO with matched GPT-4o trajectories exists (54.1 vs. 75.2), but the reasoning traces are not matched in length/quality analysis.

Improvement claims are inconsistent with the tables. The text claims 'consistent improvements across all settings,' yet for LLaVA-OneVision the Ego3D gains are marginal (46.2→48.7) with several subtask drops (e.g., Ego Dist. 39.7→36.5, Travel Time 34.1→32.8); the quoted '18.1%–36.9%' range applies only to Qwen/InternVL. Percentages in the text mix relative and absolute gains confusingly (e.g., '88.9% (62.7 vs. 33.2)' is a relative figure, '21.8% (62.7 vs. 49.6)' again relative).

The qualitative visualization evidence is weak: point clouds 'roughly depict the underlying scene' with only three cherry-picked correct-answer examples shown; no quantitative evaluation of latent-to-geometry fidelity (e.g., against ground-truth geometry) is provided.

Presentation and writing issues undermine polish: a sentence in Sec. 4.3 says 'Aug-CGMap-FFR-Out performs reasoning with the augmented cognitive map ... whereas Aug-CGMap-FFR-Out relies solely on plain cognitive maps' (second instance should be Plain-); duplicate reference entries ([7]/[8], [14]/[15]); typos ('bird's-eye-vie', 'a new novel framework', 'effectively exploits'); the coined term 'mentaling' is non-standard and used inconsistently with 'mental imagery.'

Code is promised but not included, and only the qualitative evidence for the projector-based 3D recovery is in the main paper; key details (data-generation prompts, CoT statistics) are deferred to supplementary material, limiting independent verification of the strongest claims.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel and well-motivated: injecting 3D 'mental' latent tokens into the reasoning trajectory of a VLM, aligned to a 3D foundation model (VGGT) during training but requiring no external priors, depth maps, or auxiliary models at inference time (G1–G3). This is a meaningful advance over prior work that relies on BEV/cognitive-map annotations (MindCube, Ego3D) or external 3D encoders at inference (VLM-3R).

The two-stage training design (feature-distillation SFT followed by outcome-based GRPO with a 3D-alignment reward) is coherent and clearly formulated, and the reward design (format, answer, 3D cosine similarity) is sensible and well justified.

The experimental evidence is broad and convincing on the whole: results span three VLM families (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, LLaVA-OneVision-1.5) across 3B–78B scales, two held-out evaluation settings (MindCube-Tiny, Ego3D-Bench), and six additional benchmarks (Table 2) with task-specific baselines. Consistent gains across scales/architectures support the claim of general applicability, and the best model reportedly outperforms even o3 on MindCube-Tiny and edges it on Ego3D-Bench.

The ablations are informative and address the right design questions: latent token placement (positioning before/after text vs. interleaved, 75.2 vs. 42.0), projector direction (recoverable VLM-to-VGGT vs. non-recoverable compression), individual RL rewards (r3D and rans each matter substantially), and latent size (with a notable degradation at size 64). Training-strategy comparisons (Table 4) against CoT SFT, cognitive-map SFT, and GRPO-only baselines strengthen the attribution of gains to the proposed framework rather than to generic SFT/RL.

The interpretability angle—recovering point clouds from the 3D latents via the projector and VGGT's DPT head—is an attractive feature that distinguishes latent reasoning from prior opaque-latent methods, and the paper is candid about limitations (latents are not autoregressively integrated, no iterative mentaling).
weaknesses: The evaluation has a domain-overlap concern: training data is built from the 10K MindCube training split (via GPT-4o), and one of the two main benchmarks (MindCube-Tiny) is from the same source, so in-domain gains may be inflated. The cross-benchmark results (Table 2, Ego3D-Bench without Ego3D-specific data) mitigate this partially, but the paper would benefit from a clearer statement of train/test overlap and held-out-only reporting.

The margin over the strongest SFT baseline at stage 1 is modest (62.7 vs. 60.8 over Plain-CGMap-FFR-Out-SFT, 3.1 points), so the headline gains (e.g., '88.9%') rely heavily on weak base-model comparisons and relative-gain framing; absolute numbers should be foregrounded and statistical significance/variance across seeds is not reported anywhere.

The 'annotation-free' and 'no 3D prior' claims need more careful qualification: training requires VGGT feature distillation and GPT-4o-generated CoT data with hand-crafted 3D placeholder patterns. These are legitimate design choices, but the abstract's 'does not rely on explicitly labeled 3D data for training' framing undersells the dependence on a large proprietary teacher (GPT-4o), which also hurts reproducibility (exact prompts, filters, and data quality control are deferred to supplementary material).

The interpretability claim is only weakly supported: point-cloud visualizations are shown for three cherry-picked successful examples with the qualitative statement that regions 'roughly depict' the scene. No quantitative evaluation of reconstruction quality (e.g., Chamfer distance, depth error) or of whether reasoning actually consults the 3D content (e.g., counterfactual latent perturbations) is provided.

Some results complicate the story and deserve more analysis: Travel Time degrades on Ego3D-Bench; the smallest models (LLaVA-O-4B/8B) gain little from stage 2 (48.1/48.7 vs. 47.4/46.9); and the latent-size ablation collapses catastrophically at size 64 (15.5), suggesting the method is fragile and the mechanism not fully understood.

Presentation has a number of errors that should be fixed: typos ('bird's-eye-vie', 'a new novel framework', 'Aug-CGMap-FFR-Out... whereas Aug-CGMap-FFR-Out' should be 'Plain-'), unbalanced parentheses in Eq. (7), inconsistent notation in Eq. (11) (mean over r_{1,t},...,r_{N,t} but std written as r_{i,t},...,r_{N,t}), and the non-standard term 'mentaling' used without definition. Table 3 lacks absolute clarity on which training data 3DThinker used for the Ego3D-VLM comparison.

No inference-overhead analysis: the framework adds k latent tokens per trajectory; a token/cost comparison against pure-text CoT and tool-based baselines would strengthen the 'intrinsic, no external overhead' positioning.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: injecting 3D latent tokens into the reasoning trajectory of VLMs, moving beyond pure-text and 2D 'thinking with image' paradigms, is an original contribution distinct from Mirage [80] and cognitive-map methods like MindCube/Ego3D-VLM.

Extensive and convincing empirical support: consistent gains across 8+ base VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, InternVL3, LLaVA-OneVision-1.5, including a MoE variant) and many benchmarks (MindCube-Tiny, Ego3D-Bench, VSI-Bench, SPBench, CV-Bench, SPAR-Bench, ViewSpatial-Bench, MMSI-Bench, 3DSRBench), with cross-dataset generalization (trained only on MindCube data, still strong on Ego3D-Bench).

The two-stage design (VGGT feature distillation via an interpretable VLM-to-VGGT projector, followed by outcome-based GRPO that also refines the 3D latents via a cosine-similarity reward) is technically coherent, and ablations (Tables 4-6, 11) isolate the contribution of the 3D alignment loss, token placement, latent size, and each reward.

Good interpretability story: the 3D latents can be decoded into point clouds via the projector + VGGT DPT, with qualitative examples (Figs. 4, 10-17), a quantitative prompt-relevance density check (Sec. 8.4), and a candid failure-case analysis (Sec. 14.2).

Thorough supplementary material: dataset construction prompts, training curves, cost analysis, ablations on projection direction and 3D loss, and an honest clarification of what 'annotation-free' means.
weaknesses: A key confound is not fully controlled: the CoT data is generated by GPT-4.1 with the ground-truth answer R as input (Eq. 1), so the supervised gains may partly reflect distillation of a strong teacher's (answer-informed) reasoning rather than the 3D mentaling itself. The 'w/o L3D' ablation (62.7 vs 54.1) and CoT-SFT baseline (53.4) partially mitigate this, but a teacher-CoT SFT without answer leakage, or with matched token budget, is not reported.

The claim of 'intrinsic 3D mentaling' is somewhat overstated: VGGT (an external 3D foundation model) is required during training, and the latents are not autoregressively consumed by the model (placed at the start of the trajectory; their hidden states are only read out at the end for projection), so the causal role of the 3D latent in producing the answer is not definitively established (acknowledged as a limitation in Sec. 13).
No variance/statistical significance reporting (single-run numbers, no seeds/std), despite large-scale RL training where run-to-run variance can be substantial.

Some results raise interpretability questions: latent sizes of 32/64 collapse to near-random accuracy (Table 5), and the 'prompt-relevant region' claim is supported by only one quantitative density example (Sec. 8.4).

Presentation issues: occasional textual errors (e.g., the Aug-CGMap-FFR-Out description in Sec. 4.3 contradicts itself; Eq. 12 has a formatting error), heavy reliance on 'Supp. Mat.' pointers, and minor notational sloppiness that slightly hampers reproducibility of the exact training recipe.

The RL stage still uses an r3D reward computed against frozen VGGT features, which is arguably not purely 'outcome-driven'; the paper's framing of stage 2 as outcome-only is somewhat inconsistent with Eq. 12.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and reasonably novel: injecting a 3D latent 'mentaling' step into VLM reasoning by aligning special-token hidden states with features from a 3D foundation model (VGGT), extending latent visual reasoning (e.g., Mirage) from 2D image latents to 3D geometry, without external priors at inference.

The two-stage training recipe (SFT with 3D alignment + textual losses, followed by GRPO with a composite reward) is clearly described, and the projector design that maps VLM latents into VGGT space enables recovery of point clouds, giving the framework a concrete interpretability story (Fig. 4, Figs. 10-16).

The experimental breadth is substantial: multiple base model families (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-OneVision-1.5), multiple scales, and many benchmarks (MindCube-Tiny, Ego3D-Bench, VSI-Bench, SPBench, CV-Bench, SPAR-Bench, ViewSpatial-Bench, MMSI-Bench, 3DSRBench), with consistent gains over baselines.

Ablations are informative: token placement (75.2 vs. 42.0 for mid-trajectory placement), latent size, reward components, projection direction, and removal of the 3D alignment loss (62.7 vs. 54.1) all shed light on the design; the ablation without r_3D (68.3) supports that the gains are not purely teacher-dependent.
General image understanding is largely preserved (Table 10), and failure-case analysis (Fig. 17) is honest and insightful, tracing an error to the reconstructed point cloud.
weaknesses: Potential train-test contamination undermines headline claims. The 'Large-Scale Curated Dataset' used for the starred models in Tables 2 and 10 is built from MM-Spatial, SPAR, MindCube, and SpatialLadder - sources that overlap with (or are closely related to) the evaluation benchmarks SPAR-Bench, SPBench, and MindCube-Tiny. The strongest claims (beating SpatialLadder, VILASR, and o3) rest on these models, so the comparisons are not clearly apples-to-apples.

The very large gains on MindCube-Tiny (e.g., +108.8% overall) are partly expected since the MindCube-only models are trained on 10K samples drawn from the same source dataset that MindCube-Tiny is derived from; cross-dataset results (Ego3D-Bench) are more convincing but show smaller margins, sometimes comparable to Ego3D-VLM (Table 3: 68.0 vs. 68.0 at 38B).

Overclaimed 'annotation-free' and 'outcome-only' framing. CoT data is generated by GPT-4.1 conditioned on ground-truth answers (Fig. 8), which yields post-hoc rationalizations rather than faithful reasoning; and Stage 2 is not purely outcome-driven since r_3D is computed against frozen VGGT teacher features (Eq. 12), contradicting the abstract's claim of optimizing 'solely based on outcome signals'. The supplement (Sec. 11) partially concedes this.

The mechanistic contribution of the 3D latent itself is not fully isolated: without the 3D alignment loss, performance is 54.1 vs. CoT SFT's 53.4, suggesting a large fraction of the improvement comes from SFT on GPT-4.1-generated CoT plus extra token capacity rather than genuine geometric mentaling. The point-cloud visualizations are qualitatively suggestive but coarse, and no quantitative 3D-reconstruction fidelity metric is reported.

Brittleness is evident: performance collapses at latent sizes of 32/64 (25.1/15.5), and mid-trajectory token placement is catastrophic (42.0), indicating the method works only in a narrow configuration; robustness of the recipe to other settings is unclear.

Presentation and consistency issues: the abstract's code link is empty; Eq. 12 has a formatting error; Sec. 4.3 contains a typo where both cognitive-map baselines are described as 'Aug-CGMap-FFR-Out'; relative vs. absolute improvements are sometimes conflated in the text; and the claims of being 'the first' to think with 3D should be softened given prior 3D-token works (e.g., VLM-3R).

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem—3D spatial reasoning from limited views—and the proposed 'think with 3D mentaling' idea (distilling 3D foundation model features into latent tokens embedded in the reasoning trajectory) is a fresh and sensible combination of latent reasoning and 3D representation learning.

The two-stage training design (feature-alignment SFT followed by outcome-driven GRPO with a frozen projector and an auxiliary 3D-alignment reward) is technically well-specified, with clear loss formulations (Eqs. 2-12), and the design choices are supported by ablations (token position, latent size, projector direction, individual rewards, and removal of L_3D).

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: 8+ base VLMs across three model families (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-OneVision-1.5), two main benchmarks (MindCube-Tiny, Ego3D-Bench) plus six additional spatial benchmarks (Tab. 2), comparisons against external-prior methods (Ego3D-VLM) and cognitive-map baselines (Tab. 3, Tab. 4), and evidence that general image understanding is preserved (Tab. 10).

The claim that no dense 3D annotation is needed is largely substantiated: supervision comes from a 3D foundation model (VGGT) rather than manual geometry labels, and the ablation shows the model retains gains (68.3 vs. 62.7) even without the r_3D reward at RL time.

Interpretability is addressed beyond rhetoric: the projector allows recovery of point clouds from the 3D latents (Figs. 4, 10-17), a prompt-relevant density analysis is provided (Sec. 8.4), and a failure case is analyzed honestly (Sec. 14.2).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to Mirage [80]: the core mechanism (special latent tokens inside a CoT trajectory, supervised alignment to a teacher feature space, then outcome RL) is directly inherited; the main difference is replacing 2D image latents with VGGT-distilled 3D latents. The 'first to introduce think with 3D mentaling' framing is somewhat overstated given this lineage.

There is residual ambiguity about whether the 3D latent genuinely encodes geometry versus merely adding extra representational capacity: the w/o L_3D ablation (62.7 vs. 54.1, and CoT SFT at 53.4) shows special tokens alone contribute meaningfully, and removing r_3D at RL still yields 68.3. Quantitative validation of the recovered point clouds is limited to a single-scene density number (Sec. 8.4) rather than a standard reconstruction metric.

The 3D latent is not autoregressively fed back into the computation (acknowledged in Sec. 13); it functions partly as a representation-level regularizer on the trajectory rather than an intrinsic 'mentaling' loop, which weakens the cognitive-narrative claims in the abstract and introduction.

Fairness of some comparisons is unclear: the starred models in Tab. 2 are trained on a 237K curated dataset, while many compared baselines (SpatialLadder, VILASR, etc.) may use different training data; a data-matched comparison or explicit discussion is missing in the main text.

The CoT generation conditions on the ground-truth answer (Eq. 1: o = M(Q, I, R)), which is standard but should be more transparently discussed, since the supervised reasoning traces encode answer information; the relationship between the MindCube 10K training split and the MindCube-Tiny evaluation split also warrants explicit confirmation of no overlap.

The headline claim of outperforming o3 rests on a marginal gap (73.3 vs. 73.0 on Ego3D-Bench), and the consistency of the improvement across subtasks is uneven (e.g., Travel Time regressions are attributed to normalization effects without direct evidence).

Presentation issues remain: the code URL in the abstract is empty, there are typos and a mislabeled baseline description in Sec. 4.3 ('Aug-CGMap-FFR-Out relies solely on plain cognitive maps' duplicates the earlier description), and the paper leans heavily on supplementary material for essential training details.
